cell.label: History, including: quality of symptoms; timing/duration; provoking/palliating factors; associated symptoms; medical and psychological problems; risk factors for cerebrovascular and cardiovascular disease; medication use. Directed physical examination may include: general appearance; orthostatic measurements; head and neck; cardiovascular; neurological; hearing tests (Weber, Rinne to determine whether hearing loss is sensorineural); provocative tests: Dix-Hallpike (Nylen-Barany). Directed tests: glucose, if diabetic; cardiac rhythm monitoring in patients >45 years old; consider other directed tests: complete blood count, serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen.
*Potentially serious cause of dizziness? Any one of the following: Older patient (age >70 years) No vertigo Neurological deficit
Vertigo?
Consider psychogenic dizziness: - Screen for anxiety, panic, depression Reconsider serious causes of dizziness* Consider other etiologies: - Anemia - Dehydration - Autonomic dysregulation - Etc.
Findings consistent with migraine?
Consider peripheral vestibular disorder, especially if: - Positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver, and - Nausea or vomiting
Migraine
Hearing loss?
Is dizziness persistent or episodic?
Persistent suggests vestibular neuronitis Episodic suggests benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Reconsider other peripheral vestibular disorders Reconsider serious causes of dizziness* Consider other etiologies: - Central vertigo - Perilymphatic fistula - Middle ear pathology - Etc.
Is dizziness persistent or episodic?
Persistent suggests labyrinthitis Episodic suggests Meniere's disease, especially if with - aural fullness - progressive hearing loss
Either of the following: - Neurological deficit, including progressive or unexplained hearing loss - Vertigo and high risk for cerebrovascular disease, including age
Findings suggest cardiovascular disease, which may include - Presyncope - Palpitations - Episodic nature - Cardiovascular risk factors - Arrhythmia
Findings consistent with medication-related dizziness?
Consider: - Arrhythmia monitoring - Carotid stimulation - Valsalva maneuver - Other (echocardiogram, stress test, etc.)
Findings consistent with seizure or other neurological disease?
Discontinue medication
Consider psychogenic dizziness Consider other etiologies Reconsider serious causes of dizziness*
Workup as appropriate; consider EEG, MRI, and/or referral
Neuroimaging: brain MRI preferred; consider MRA or conventional angiogram
If no diagnostic findings, continue as for vertigo.

footnotes.footnote: *Remember: Multiple etiologies common, especially in elderly—unknown cause in 10%-25% of patients.
Adapted from Kentala E, Rauch SD. A practical assessment algorithm for diagnosis of dizziness. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2003;128:54–59.

Stoffers HE, Kester AD, Kaiser V Rinkens PE, Knottnerus JA. Diagnostic value of signs and symptoms associated with peripheral arterial occlusive disease seen in general practice: a multivariable approach. Med Decis Making 1997;17:61–70.
